platforms.title: Gout vs. Pseudogout: It's Not Always the Big Toe
platforms.meta_description: Woke up with a joint suddenly swollen and throbbing and jumped straight to gout? How the ACR tells it apart from pseudogout, by joint and age.
platforms.body_html:
Woke up with a joint suddenly swollen and throbbing and jumped straight to gout? The American College of Rheumatology (ACR) explains that gout and pseudogout come from entirely different types of crystals building up in the joint. Mixing the two up can mean ending up on completely the wrong long-term treatment.

Why the same acute joint pain has different causes

Gout is acute inflammation caused by urate crystals building up in a joint when blood uric acid levels run high. It most commonly starts in the big toe but can also hit the ankle or knee, and often flares suddenly after eating purine-rich meat or seafood, or after drinking alcohol.

Pseudogout comes from an entirely different crystal. It's marked by calcium pyrophosphate crystals building up in joint cartilage, producing the same kind of acute swelling and pain as gout. It tends to show up in the knee or wrist, and is more often triggered by surgery, trauma, or another acute illness rather than by any particular food.

How to tell them apart, and what to check

First, which joint the pain started in. The ACR notes that acute pain starting in the big toe is more likely gout, while pain starting in the knee or wrist leans more toward pseudogout.

Second, your age and what happened recently. Pseudogout is far more common past age 60 and often shows up suddenly right after surgery, trauma, or another illness. Gout can appear at a relatively younger age, and there's usually a clear pattern of symptoms flaring the day after a particular food or drinking bout.

What matters most is not restarting old gout medication on your own without an accurate diagnosis. Gout needs long-term treatment aimed at lowering uric acid, but pseudogout has nothing to do with uric acid, so that kind of medication does nothing for it at all. For both conditions, the gold-standard way to confirm the diagnosis is drawing joint fluid and checking the crystal shape under a polarized microscope, so getting properly tested during a flare is the most reliable way forward.

When it's hard to tell which one is going on, it helps to note exactly which joint the pain started in, what you ate or drank recently, and whether you've had any recent surgery or trauma. Anti-inflammatory medication calms the acute pain for both conditions, but the long-term management is completely different, so pinning down the actual cause matters.

It's also worth mentioning any other health conditions during that visit, since pseudogout shows up more often alongside issues like an underactive thyroid or excess iron storage, while gout tends to travel together with high blood pressure, obesity, or kidney trouble. Bringing up any of those existing conditions can help a doctor narrow things down more quickly, even before the test results actually come back from the lab.

Talk to a doctor about getting joint fluid tested if it's unclear which one you're dealing with, rather than assuming based on the pain alone.
